proofs.proof_tex:
Because \(I\) is compact, \(|Z|\leq \operatorname{diam}(I)\) almost surely.  The no-stayer condition gives \(|Z|>0\) almost surely, and hence
\[
0<A=E_P|Z|\leq \operatorname{diam}(I)<\infty.
\]
Observed integrability also gives \(E_P|\Delta Y|<\infty\), so \(T\) is finite.

First take \(Q\in\mathfrak Q(P)\), and write \(m=m_Q\).  Consistency gives the pointwise decomposition
\[
\Delta Y
=Y_2^Q(D_2)-Y_1^Q(D_1)
=\{Y_2^Q(D_2)-Y_2^Q(D_1)\}
 +\{Y_2^Q(D_1)-Y_1^Q(D_1)\}.
\]
The jointly measurable version in conditional parallel trends may be evaluated at \(D_1=X\); therefore
\[
E_Q[Y_2^Q(D_1)-Y_1^Q(D_1)\mid X,Z]=m(X).
\]
The observed-law match then implies, for \(P_{XZ}\)-almost every \((x,z)\),
\[
g(x,z)-m(x)
=E_Q[Y_2^Q(D_2)-Y_2^Q(D_1)\mid X=x,Z=z].
\]
The mean-movement bound yields
\[
|g(x,z)-m(x)|\leq K|z|\qquad P_{XZ}\text{-almost everywhere}.
\]
Both sides define continuous functions on \(H\): continuity of \(g\) is assumed and continuity of \(m\) is part of the legal-completion definition.  If the displayed inequality failed at a point of \(H=\operatorname{supp}_P(X,Z)\), it would fail on a relatively open neighborhood of that point; every such neighborhood has positive \(P_{XZ}\)-probability, a contradiction.  Thus it holds everywhere on \(H\).  The trend bound and trend Lipschitz condition now show \(m\in\mathcal C_P\).  This proves
\[
\mathfrak Q(P)\neq\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal C_P\neq\varnothing.
\]

The same decomposition identifies the value associated with any legal completion.  By iterated expectations and the definition of \(\nu_P\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A\theta(Q)
&=E_Q\!\left[S\{Y_2^Q(D_2)-Y_2^Q(D_1)\}\right]\\
&=E_P[S\Delta Y]-E_Q\!\left[S\{Y_2^Q(D_1)-Y_1^Q(D_1)\}\right]\\
&=T-E_P[S m(X)]
=T-\int_{X_0}m(x)\,d\nu_P(x)
=T-J_P(m).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently every legal value belongs to \(\Theta(P)\).

Conversely, fix \(u\in\mathcal C_P\) and retain the observed vector with law \(P\).  Since \(P(Z=0)=0\), define
\[
b_u=\frac{g(X,Z)-u(X)}{Z}
\]
off the null event \(\{Z=0\}\), and set it equal to zero on that event.  The support inequality in the definition of \(\mathcal C_P\) gives \(|b_u|\leq K\) almost surely.  Define, simultaneously for every \(d\in I\),
\[
Y_1^{Q_u}(d)=Y_1+b_u(d-D_1),
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_u}(d)=Y_2+b_u(d-D_2).
\]
These schedules are jointly measurable.  They satisfy consistency pointwise:
\[
Y_1^{Q_u}(D_1)=Y_1,
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_u}(D_2)=Y_2.
\]
Thus the complete joint observed law, not merely its moments, remains \(P\).  For fixed \(d\in I\), compactness of \(I\) and \(|b_u|\leq K\) give
\[
|Y_t^{Q_u}(d)|\leq |Y_t|+K\operatorname{diam}(I),
\]
so latent integrability follows from observed integrability.  Both schedules are individually \(K\)-Lipschitz because
\[
|Y_t^{Q_u}(d)-Y_t^{Q_u}(d')|=|b_u|\,|d-d'|\leq K|d-d'|.
\]
Their period difference is independent of \(d\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_2^{Q_u}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u}(d)
&=\Delta Y+b_u(D_1-D_2)\\
&=\Delta Y-b_uZ
=\Delta Y-g(X,Z)+u(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(g(X,Z)=E_P[\Delta Y\mid X,Z]\),
\[
E_{Q_u}[Y_2^{Q_u}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u}(d)\mid X,Z]=u(X)
=E_{Q_u}[Y_2^{Q_u}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u}(d)\mid X]
\]
for every \(d\in I\).  This proves the stronger all-\(I\) parallel-trends equality, and setting \(d=X\) gives \(m_{Q_u}=u\).  The remaining shape restrictions on \(m_{Q_u}\) follow directly from \(u\in\mathcal C_P\).  Moreover,
\[
Y_2^{Q_u}(D_2)-Y_2^{Q_u}(D_1)=b_uZ=g(X,Z)-u(X),
\]
whose absolute conditional mean is at most \(K|Z|\).  Hence \(Q_u\in\mathfrak Q(P)\), proving the reverse nonemptiness implication.  Finally,
\[
\theta(Q_u)
=\frac{E_P[S\{g(X,Z)-u(X)\}]}{A}
=\frac{T-J_P(u)}{A},
\]
where \(E_P[Sg(X,Z)]=E_P[S\Delta Y]=T\) by iterated expectations.  Thus every point of \(\Theta(P)\) is attained by a legal full-data law, while the first part proved that no other value is legal.  This establishes the asserted full-observed-law sharp equality on the declared continuous-trend completion class; the construction itself also establishes the claimed individual schedule regularity.

The set \(X_0\) is closed as a support and is contained in compact \(I\), hence is compact.  Every \(u\in\mathcal C_P\) is bounded by \(M\) and has the common modulus
\[
|u(x)-u(x')|\leq L|x-x'|.
\]
The class is uniformly closed: if \(u_j\in\mathcal C_P\) and \(u_j\to u\) uniformly, then the level bound, every Lipschitz inequality, and every support-cone inequality pass to the limit, so \(u\in\mathcal C_P\).  To see compactness without an additional premise, choose a countable dense subset of compact \(X_0\).  Boundedness permits a diagonal subsequence converging on that subset; the common Lipschitz modulus makes the subsequence uniformly Cauchy on \(X_0\), and its uniform limit lies in \(\mathcal C_P\) by closedness.  Thus \(\mathcal C_P\) is sequentially compact, and therefore compact in the metric uniform norm.  All defining inequalities are convex, so \(\mathcal C_P\) is convex.

For every finite Borel partition \((B_j)_j\) of \(X_0\),
\[
\sum_j|\nu_P(B_j)|
=\sum_j|E_P[S\mathbf 1\{X\in B_j\}]|
\leq E_P\sum_j\mathbf 1\{X\in B_j\}=1.
\]
Taking the supremum over partitions gives \(\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq1\).  Hence
\[
|J_P(u)-J_P(v)|\leq\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\|u-v\|_\infty
\leq\|u-v\|_\infty,
\]
so \(J_P\) is continuous.  Its minimum and maximum on nonempty compact \(\mathcal C_P\) are therefore attained.  The continuous linear image of the convex set \(\mathcal C_P\) is an interval, and compactness closes its endpoints; consequently
\[
J_P(\mathcal C_P)=[V_P^-,V_P^+].
\]
Because \(A>0\), the affine map \(v\mapsto(T-v)/A\) reverses endpoints, and full-law sharpness yields
\[
\Theta(P)=\left[\frac{T-V_P^+}{A},\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}\right].
\]
Finally, for every \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), iterated expectations and its cone restriction give
\[
|T-J_P(u)|
=|E_P[S\{g(X,Z)-u(X)\}]|
\leq E_P|g(X,Z)-u(X)|
\leq K E_P|Z|=KA.
\]
Division by the positive \(A\) proves \(\Theta(P)\subseteq[-K,K]\).

For \((d,z)\in H\), the functions of \(x\)
\[
g(d,z)-K|z|-L|x-d|
\quad\text{and}\quad
g(d,z)+K|z|+L|x-d|
\]
are \(L\)-Lipschitz.  Suprema, infima, maxima, and minima of finite-valued functions sharing the same Lipschitz constant retain that constant.  Compactness of \(H\) and continuity of \(g\) make all displayed envelopes finite.  Thus \(\ell_P\) and \(r_P\) are continuous and \(L\)-Lipschitz.

If \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), then for every \((d,z)\in H\) and \(x\in X_0\),
\[
u(x)\geq u(d)-L|x-d|
\geq g(d,z)-K|z|-L|x-d|,
\]
and \(u(x)\geq-M\).  Taking the supremum and maximum proves \(u\geq\ell_P\).  Similarly,
\[
u(x)\leq u(d)+L|x-d|
\leq g(d,z)+K|z|+L|x-d|,
\]
together with \(u(x)\leq M\), proves \(u\leq r_P\).

Conversely, suppose \(u\) is continuous, \(\operatorname{Lip}(u)\leq L\), and \(\ell_P\leq u\leq r_P\).  The definitions give \(\ell_P\geq-M\) and \(r_P\leq M\), so \(\|u\|_\infty\leq M\).  At each \((d,z)\in H\),
\[
\ell_P(d)\geq g(d,z)-K|z|,
\qquad
r_P(d)\leq g(d,z)+K|z|.
\]
Therefore
\[
g(d,z)-K|z|\leq u(d)\leq g(d,z)+K|z|,
\]
which is exactly the observed cone restriction.  This proves
\[
\mathcal C_P
=\{u\in C(X_0):\operatorname{Lip}(u)\leq L, \ell_P\leq u\leq r_P\}.
\]

Nonemptiness plainly implies \(\ell_P\leq r_P\).  Conversely, if \(\ell_P\leq r_P\), take \(u=\ell_P\).  It is \(L\)-Lipschitz, satisfies \(\ell_P\leq u\leq r_P\), and hence belongs to \(\mathcal C_P\) by the characterization just proved.  Thus the pointwise envelope inequality is also sufficient.

Under \(P^{\circ}\), the first rectangle has area \(1/2\) and density \(2p_{\circ}\), hence mass \(p_{\circ}\); the second has area \(1/2\) and density \(2(1-p_{\circ})\), hence mass \(1-p_{\circ}\).  Both densities are finite and strictly positive because \(p_{\circ}\in(0,1)\).  The outcomes vanish and are therefore uniformly bounded.  Absolute continuity gives \(P^{\circ}(Z=0)=0\).  On the second rectangle, every neighborhood of zero in the \(z\)-coordinate has positive probability, so
\[
P^{\circ}(|Z|\leq\eta)>0\qquad\text{for every }\eta>0.
\]
This is the source's marginal quasi-stayer requirement.  In contrast, for every \(x\in[-1,0)\), the conditional support of \(Z\) is \([1/2,1]\), and hence
\[
P^{\circ}(|Z|\leq\eta\mid X=x)=0
\qquad(0<\eta<1/2).
\]
Since the first rectangle has mass \(p_{\circ}\), the failure region has precisely that baseline probability.

For either sign \(s\in\{+,-\}\), the definition gives, outside the null event \(Z=0\),
\[
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)=u_s^{\circ}(X)
\qquad\text{for every }d\in[-2,2].
\]
Thus the schedules are static, their period difference has conditional mean \(u_s^{\circ}(X)\) given either \((X,Z)\) or \(X\), and parallel trends holds on the baseline support and indeed on all of \(I\).  At the observed doses,
\[
Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_1)=0=Y_1,
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_2)=0=Y_2,
\]
so both laws match the full observed law.  The function \(u_s^{\circ}\) is bounded by one and is one-Lipschitz.  On \([-1,0]\), \(|u_s^{\circ}(X)|\leq1/2\leq Z\), while on \([0,1]\) it vanishes.  Therefore each schedule slope \(-u_s^{\circ}(X)/Z\) is bounded in absolute value by one, which proves latent integrability on compact \(I\) and the conditional mean-movement bound.  These verifications establish the substantive staticity, consistency, support, slope, and parallel-trends clauses invoked from the source's Assumptions 1--4.

The signed baseline measure is supported only by the first rectangle because \(S=1\) there and the conditional sign mean is zero on the symmetric second rectangle.  Hence
\[
d\nu_{P^{\circ}}(x)=p_{\circ}\mathbf 1\{x\in[-1,0]\}\,dx.
\]
Also \(T=0\), and
\[
A=p_{\circ}\frac34+(1-p_{\circ})\frac18
=\frac{1+5p_{\circ}}8.
\]
Since
\[
\int_{-1}^0\min\{-x,1/2\}\,dx=\frac38,
\]
the two completions have
\[
\theta(Q_+^{\circ})=-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
\qquad
\theta(Q_-^{\circ})=\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}}.
\]
They share the same observed law but have different WAOSS values.  Thus marginal quasi-stayers cannot imply the baseline-conditional positivity used immediately before the cited display, and cannot by themselves identify the asserted singleton.

For each positive integer \(k\), let
\[
q_k(x)=P(|Z|\leq 1/k\mid X=x).
\]
The stated condition is exactly \(q_k(X)>0\) almost surely for every \(k\).  Fix \(x\in X_0\) and an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x\).  By the definition of support, \(P(X\in U)>0\).  Since \(q_k>0\) for \(P_X\)-almost every baseline,
\[
P(X\in U,|Z|\leq1/k)
=\int_Uq_k(x')\,dP_X(x')>0.
\]
It follows that \(H\) meets \(U\times[-1/k,1/k]\).  Taking neighborhoods shrinking to \(x\), choosing one such support point for each \(k\), and using closedness of the compact support \(H\) proves
\[
(x,0)\in H\qquad\text{for every }x\in X_0.
\]
No conditioning on a null singleton is used in this support argument.

For any \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), the observed cone restriction at \((x,0)\) gives
\[
|g(x,0)-u(x)|\leq K|0|=0,
\]
so \(u(x)=g(x,0)\) for all \(x\in X_0\).  Compatibility guarantees that this function is feasible; hence
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{x\mapsto g(x,0)\},
\qquad
V_P^-=V_P^+=\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x),
\qquad
R(P)=0.
\]
Full-law sharpness then gives the singleton
\[
\Theta(P)=\left\{\frac{T-\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x)}{A}\right\}.
\]
This is the weighted WAOSS quasi-stayer formula.  The proposition's comparison to the earlier unweighted target \(\delta_1\) is only a distinction of estimands: no equality with \(\delta_1\) is used or asserted.  Finally, the continuous support-hole law in the marginal-gap proposition has a positive-probability baseline region without zero in its conditional support and produces two distinct legal values, so failure of the conditional condition can indeed yield \(R(P)>0\).  No claim that support failure is sufficient for \(R(P)>0\) is needed.

At the two atoms of \(P^{\diamond}\),
\[
(X,Z)=(-1/2,1/2)\quad\text{and}\quad(X,Z)=(1/2,-1/2),
\]
each with probability \(1/2\).  Thus
\[
X_0=\{-1/2,1/2\},
\qquad
H=\{(-1/2,1/2),(1/2,-1/2)\}.
\]
Because \(Y_1=Y_2=0\), \(g=0\) and \(T=0\), while
\[
A=E|Z|=\frac12,
\qquad
\nu_P=\frac12\delta_{-1/2}-\frac12\delta_{1/2}.
\]
With \(K=L=M=1\), the local cone at either baseline is \([-1/2,1/2]\).  Propagating the other baseline's cone across distance one cannot tighten this interval.  Direct substitution in the obstacle formulas therefore gives
\[
\ell_P(-1/2)=\ell_P(1/2)=-\frac12,
\qquad
r_P(-1/2)=r_P(1/2)=\frac12.
\]
The largest possible difference between two values in these intervals is one, so the one-Lipschitz condition adds no restriction.  Hence
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{u:|u(-1/2)|\leq1/2, |u(1/2)|\leq1/2\}.
\]
For such \(u\),
\[
J_P(u)=\frac{u(-1/2)-u(1/2)}2,
\qquad
\frac{T-J_P(u)}A=u(1/2)-u(-1/2).
\]
Its attained range is \([-1,1]\), proving \(\Theta(P)=[-1,1]\).

The displayed slope equals
\[
b_u^{\diamond}=
\begin{cases}
-2u(-1/2),&X=-1/2,\\
2u(1/2),&X=1/2,
\end{cases}
\]
and therefore \(|b_u^{\diamond}|\leq1\).  Evaluation at \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) gives the two observed zeros, so the complete observed law is preserved.  For every \(d\in[-1,1]\), direct subtraction gives
\[
Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)=u(X).
\]
Thus parallel trends holds conditionally on \((X,Z)\) and on \(X\), both on the baseline support and on all of \(I\), and \(m_{Q_u^{\diamond}}=u\).  The movement is \(b_u^{\diamond}Z=-u(X)\), so its magnitude is at most \(|Z|\); all legal restrictions follow.  The target is the value computed above.  If \(u(-1/2)=1/2\) and \(u(1/2)=-1/2\), then \(b_u^{\diamond}=-1\) at both atoms and \(\theta=-1\).  Reversing the signs gives \(b_u^{\diamond}=1\) and \(\theta=1\).  Both signs of treatment change and both baseline values are used, so this is not a common-baseline scalar design.

The two rectangles in the definition have respective areas \(1/2\) and \(1/2\).  Their density integrals are \(p_{\circ}\) and \(1-p_{\circ}\), so they define a probability law.  Since \(p_{\circ}\in(0,1)\), the density is bounded and strictly positive on each support rectangle.  The outcomes are zero, exact stayers form a Lebesgue-null set, and the second rectangle gives positive probability to every set \(\{|Z|\leq\eta\}\) with \(\eta>0\).  For each \(x\in[-1,0)\), however, the conditional support is \([1/2,1]\), so conditional quasi-stayers fail there.  Integrating the first rectangle over \(z\) shows that this baseline region has probability \(p_{\circ}\).

The definitions immediately yield
\[
X_0=[-1,1],
\qquad
H=[-1,0]\times[1/2,1]\ \cup\ [0,1]\times[-1/4,1/4],
\qquad
g=0,
\qquad
T=0.
\]
On the first rectangle \(S=1\); on the second, the conditional distribution of \(Z\) is symmetric.  Hence
\[
d\nu_P(x)=p_{\circ}\mathbf 1\{x\in[-1,0]\}\,dx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
A=p_{\circ}E[Z\mid Z\in[1/2,1]]
+(1-p_{\circ})E[|Z|\mid Z\in[-1/4,1/4]]
=\frac{3p_{\circ}}4+\frac{1-p_{\circ}}8
=\frac{1+5p_{\circ}}8.
\]

For \(x\in[0,1]\), the support contains \((x,0)\), so the cone at zero forces both obstacles to equal zero.  For \(x\in[-1,0]\), the local smallest change gives \(|u(x)|\leq1/2\), while the one-Lipschitz connection to \(u(0)=0\) gives \(|u(x)|\leq-x\).  Substitution in the envelope formulas shows these are the only restrictions:
\[
r_P(x)=-\ell_P(x)=
\begin{cases}
\min\{-x,1/2\},&x\in[-1,0],\\
0,&x\in[0,1].
\end{cases}
\]
Both envelope functions are feasible.  Therefore the extrema of the signed objective are
\[
V_P^{\pm}=\mathbin{\pm}p_{\circ}\int_{-1}^0\min\{-x,1/2\}\,dx
=\mathbin{\pm}\frac{3p_{\circ}}8,
\]
with the usual convention that \(V_P^+\) takes the plus sign.  The attained-interval formula now gives
\[
\Theta(P^{\circ})
=\left[-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
          \frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}}\right].
\]

For \(s\in\{+,-\}\), evaluation of the displayed schedules at observed doses gives
\[
Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_1)=0,
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_2)=0,
\]
so the entire observed law is preserved.  Their difference is, for every \(d\in[-2,2]\),
\[
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)=u_s^{\circ}(X).
\]
This proves both baseline-support and all-\(I\) parallel trends and gives \(m_{Q_s^{\circ}}=u_s^{\circ}\).  The functions are bounded and one-Lipschitz.  Also \(|u_s^{\circ}(X)|\leq|Z|\) on both rectangles, so the common schedule slope has magnitude at most one and the conditional movement bound holds.  Thus both laws are legal.  Finally,
\[
\theta(Q_+^{\circ})=-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
\qquad
\theta(Q_-^{\circ})=\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
\]
as asserted.

Assume \(\mathcal C_P\neq\varnothing\).  Obstacle compatibility gives \(\ell_P\leq r_P\), and both obstacles are \(L\)-Lipschitz.  If \(v\in\mathcal C_P^{\varepsilon}\), the same propagation used for the exact obstacle characterization, now with the relaxed cone, gives
\[
\ell_P(x)-\varepsilon\leq v(x)\leq r_P(x)+\varepsilon
\qquad(x\in X_0).
\]
Indeed, the unrelaxed level constraints handle the constant obstacle pieces and each relaxed support inequality contributes at most \(\varepsilon\).  Pointwise projection onto the interval \([\ell_P(x),r_P(x)]\) is exactly \(\Pi_P(v)(x)\); hence
\[
|v(x)-\Pi_P(v)(x)|\leq\varepsilon.
\]
The maximum or minimum of two real-valued \(L\)-Lipschitz functions is again \(L\)-Lipschitz, as follows from
\[
|\max\{a,b\}-\max\{c,d\}|\leq\max\{|a-c|,|b-d|\},
\]
and the analogous inequality for minima.  Therefore \(\Pi_P(v)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and lies between the exact obstacles.  Obstacle compatibility implies
\[
\Pi_P(v)\in\mathcal C_P,
\qquad
\|v-\Pi_P(v)\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon.
\]
The factor one cannot be reduced: take a singleton \(X_0\), one support point with nonzero \(z\), \(g=0\), \(K=0\), and \(M\geq\varepsilon\).  Then \(\mathcal C_P=\{0\}\), while the relaxed class contains the constant \(v=\varepsilon\), whose distance to \(\mathcal C_P\) is exactly \(\varepsilon\).

For the mesh class, omission of constraints implies
\[
\ell_{P,h}\leq\ell_P\leq r_P\leq r_{P,h}.
\]
Any fixed member of \(\mathcal C_P\) lies between \(\ell_{P,h}\) and \(r_{P,h}\), so the mesh obstacles are ordered and both \(\ell_{P,h}\) and \(r_{P,h}\) belong to \(\mathcal C_{P,h}\).  Also \(\mathcal C_P\subseteq\mathcal C_{P,h}\).  For any \(v\in\mathcal C_{P,h}\), exact clipping gives a member of \(\mathcal C_P\), and pointwise
\[
|v-\Pi_P(v)|
\leq\max\{\ell_P-\ell_{P,h},r_{P,h}-r_P\}
\leq e_h.
\]
Thus the Hausdorff distance is at most \(e_h\).  Conversely, for every \(u\in\mathcal C_P\),
\[
\|u-\ell_{P,h}\|_\infty
\geq\|\ell_P-\ell_{P,h}\|_\infty,
\qquad
\|u-r_{P,h}\|_\infty
\geq\|r_{P,h}-r_P\|_\infty,
\]
because \(u\geq\ell_P\) and \(u\leq r_P\).  The two mesh obstacles therefore attain the two lower bounds, proving
\[
d_H(\mathcal C_{P,h},\mathcal C_P)=e_h.
\]
Finally, if two nonempty compact classes are within Hausdorff distance \(e_h\), continuity of \(J_P\) and \(\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq1\) give, for either the maximum or minimum support value,
\[
|V_h-V_P|\leq\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}e_h.
\]

Fix \(w=(d,z)\in H\), and choose \(w_j=(d_j,z_j)\in H_h\) in the same connected component with \(\|w-w_j\|_\infty\leq h\).  The within-component H\"older condition and the elementary inequalities for absolute values give
\[
\begin{aligned}
|g(d,z)-g(d_j,z_j)|&\leq Gh^\beta,\\
\bigl||z|-|z_j|\bigr|&\leq h,\\
\bigl||x-d|-|x-d_j|\bigr|&\leq h.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently every term in the full lower-envelope supremum is within
\[
Gh^\beta+(K+L)h=\bar e_h
\]
of a mesh term, and the same calculation applies to the upper-envelope infimum.  Since mesh terms are a subset of full terms,
\[
0\leq\ell_P-\ell_{P,h}\leq\bar e_h,
\qquad
0\leq r_{P,h}-r_P\leq\bar e_h,
\]
uniformly on \(X_0\).  Thus \(e_h\leq\bar e_h\).

Restriction to \(B_h\) maps \(\mathcal C_{P,h}\) into \(\mathcal U_h^{\mathrm{out}}\).  Conversely, by the defining properties of the bounded McShane extension, every \(v\in\mathcal U_h^{\mathrm{out}}\) has an extension \(E_hv\) which agrees with \(v\) on \(B_h\), is bounded by \(M\), and is \(L\)-Lipschitz.  Since each mesh cone is imposed at a baseline coordinate in \(B_h\), \(E_hv\in\mathcal C_{P,h}\).  Hence restriction and extension identify the same feasible node values.

Because \(\nu_{P,h}=(\pi_h)_\#\nu_P\),
\[
J_{P,h}^{\mathrm{out}}(v)=\int_{X_0}v(\pi_h(x))\,d\nu_P(x).
\]
The extension agrees at nodes and is \(L\)-Lipschitz, so
\[
\left|J_{P,h}^{\mathrm{out}}(v)-J_P(E_hv)\right|
\leq L\int|x-\pi_h(x)|\,d|\nu_P|(x)
\leq Lh\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\leq Lh.
\]
The finite polytope is closed and bounded in \(\mathbb R^{B_h}\), hence compact, and the linear outer objective attains both extrema.  The exact Hausdorff result for \(\mathcal C_{P,h}\) gives an additional discrepancy at most \(e_h\).  Therefore each outer extremum differs from the corresponding \(V_P^-\) or \(V_P^+\) by at most
\[
e_h+Lh\leq\bar e_h+Lh.
\]

For the inner program, \(E_hv\in\mathcal C_{P,h}\), so clipping stability gives \(\Pi_P(E_hv)\in\mathcal C_P\).  Every reported inner objective is therefore attained by an exact feasible trend.  Conversely, take any \(u\in\mathcal C_P\) and let \(v=u|_{B_h}\).  Then \(v\in\mathcal U_h^{\mathrm{out}}\).  For every \(x\in X_0\), choose its projected node \(\pi_h(x)\).  Since \(u\) and \(E_hv\) agree there,
\[
|E_hv(x)-u(x)|
\leq |E_hv(x)-v(\pi_h(x))|+|u(\pi_h(x))-u(x)|
\leq2Lh.
\]
The interval \([\ell_P(x),r_P(x)]\) contains \(u(x)\), so scalar projection onto that interval cannot increase distance from \(u(x)\).  It follows that
\[
\|\Pi_P(E_hv)-u\|_\infty\leq2Lh,
\qquad
|J_P(\Pi_P(E_hv))-J_P(u)|\leq2Lh.
\]
Thus the inner objective range is contained in the full range and approximates each of its endpoints within \(2Lh\).  Compactness of the node polytope and continuity of extension, clipping, and integration also give attainment of the inner extrema.

The WAOSS endpoint map subtracts an objective support value and divides by positive \(A\).  Combining the outer error \(\bar e_h+Lh\) and the inner error \(2Lh\), and using the common upper certificate, gives Hausdorff error at most
\[
A^{-1}(\bar e_h+2Lh).
\]
Only same-component approximation was used.  Touching rectangles lie in the same connected component; a component separated from \(z=0\) creates no division or limiting step; and the clipping argument used weak inequalities throughout.  Hence none of these boundary configurations changes the certificate.

If \(P(X=0)=1\) and \(Z>0\) almost surely, then \(S=1\), \(X_0=\{0\}\), and \(\nu_P=\delta_0\).  A trend is the single scalar \(c=u(0)\).  Its exact feasible interval is
\[
\underline c
=\max\left\{-M,\sup_{(0,z)\in H}\{g(0,z)-Kz\}\right\},
\qquad
\overline c
=\min\left\{M,\inf_{(0,z)\in H}\{g(0,z)+Kz\}\right\}.
\]
Indeed these are precisely the two obstacle values, and no cross-baseline Lipschitz inequality remains.  Since \(J_P(c)=c\), the attained-interval theorem reduces to
\[
\Theta(P)=\left[\frac{T-\overline c}{A},\frac{T-\underline c}{A}\right].
\]
This is exactly the common-zero-baseline scalar program obtained by imposing the bounded conditional-average-slope inequalities \(|g(0,z)-c|\leq Kz\).  The proposition therefore records an algebraic reduction to the cited 2024 bounded-slope WAOSS bounds and makes no novelty claim for that scalar case.

Write \(D_I=\operatorname{diam}(I)\) and \(D_X=\operatorname{diam}(X_0)\).  All constants below may depend on the fixed rectangle family, \(\beta,G,B,f_0,f_1,a_0,K,L,M,D_I\), but not on \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}\).

First construct the stated boundary-aware partition.  Subdivide the plane at every horizontal and vertical edge of every rectangle in \(\mathscr R\).  The positive-area elementary rectangles contained in \(H\) have disjoint interiors and fixed positive side lengths.  For all sufficiently small \(h_n\), subdivide an elementary side of length \(a\) into \(m=\lceil\sqrt2a/h_n\rceil\) equal pieces.  Each resulting side lies between \(h_n/(2\sqrt2)\) and \(h_n/\sqrt2\).  Thus every cell has Euclidean diameter at most \(h_n\), area at least \(h_n^2/8\), and lies in a single connected component.  Assign shared edges and corners by a fixed lexicographic half-open rule to a cell whose closure contains the point.  Touching original rectangles cause no difficulty because rectangles sharing a boundary point are in the same connected component.  This produces a deterministic Borel partition with
\[
N_n\leq C_{\mathscr R}h_n^{-2}
\]
for a fixed finite constant \(C_{\mathscr R}\).

Let \(N_C\) be the sample count in a cell \(C\).  The density lower bound and the area bound imply
\[
p_C=P\{(X,Z)\in C\}\geq f_0h_n^2/8.
\]
The elementary exponential-moment proof for a binomial lower tail gives
\[
P(N_C<np_C/2)\leq e^{-np_C/8}
\leq e^{-nf_0h_n^2/64}.
\]
Therefore, except on an event of probability at most
\[
N_ne^{-nf_0h_n^2/64}=o(1)
\]
uniformly over the class, every cell contains at least \(nf_0h_n^2/16\) observations.

Conditional on all design points, the centered variables \(\Delta Y_i-g(X_i,Z_i)\) are independent, mean zero, and lie in an interval of length at most \(4B\).  The exponential-moment bound for a bounded centered variable gives, for a cell containing \(m\) observations,
\[
P\left(\left|m^{-1}\sum_{i\in C}\{\Delta Y_i-g(X_i,Z_i)\}\right|>x\ \middle|\ (X_i,Z_i)_{i=1}^n\right)
\leq2\exp\left\{-\frac{mx^2}{8B^2}\right\}.
\]
With
\[
x=2B\sqrt{\frac{128\log(8N_n/\alpha)}{nf_0h_n^2}},
\]
the count lower bound and a union bound make the conditional failure probability no larger than \(\alpha/4\).  If \(w\) is assigned to \(C\), every design point in \(C\) is in the same component and within distance \(h_n\) of \(w\), including when \(w\) lies on an assigned boundary.  The H\"older condition therefore gives the deterministic bias bound \(Gh_n^\beta\).  We have proved
\[
P\left\{\sup_{w\in H}|\widehat g_n(w)-g(w)|\leq r_n\right\}
\geq1-\frac\alpha4-N_ne^{-nf_0h_n^2/64}
\]
uniformly over \(P\).  Since \(nh_n^2/\log n\to\infty\), the last term tends to zero.

Next control the signed objective uniformly.  Extend every bounded \(L\)-Lipschitz function on \(X_0\) to the convex hull of \(X_0\), retaining the same bounds and Lipschitz constant.  For \(f_u(s,x)=su(x)\), symmetrization with an independent copy and independent Rademacher variables \((\eta_i)\) gives directly by conditional Jensen's inequality
\[
E\sup_u|(P_n-P)f_u|
\leq2E\sup_u\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\eta_iS_i u(X_i)\right|.
\]
Conditionally on the data, \(\eta_iS_i\) are again Rademacher variables.  Writing an absolutely continuous Lipschitz extension as \(u(x)=u(a)+\int_a^xu'(t)\,dt\), with \(|u(a)|\leq M\) and \(|u'|\leq L\), and using Cauchy--Schwarz for each Rademacher sum yields
\[
E\sup_u\left|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\eta_iS_i u(X_i)\right|
\leq\frac{M+LD_X}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Replacing one observation changes the supremum by at most \(2M/n\).  Iterating the bounded-difference exponential-moment inequality therefore gives, with probability at least \(1-\alpha/2\),
\[
\sup_u|(P_n-P)f_u|
\leq\frac{2(M+LD_X)}{\sqrt n}
+M\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\alpha)}n}
\leq q_n.
\]
The last inequality follows from \(\log(8/\alpha)\geq\log8\); if \(M=0\), the class contains only the zero function and the assertion is immediate.  Since \(\mathcal C_P\) is a subclass, this proves the signed-measure part of \(\mathcal E_n(P)\).

The variables \(S\Delta Y\) and \(|Z|\) lie in intervals of lengths \(4B\) and \(D_I\), respectively.  The same bounded exponential-moment calculation gives
\[
P(|\widehat T_n-T|>t_n)\leq\alpha/8,
\qquad
P(|\widehat A_n-A|>a_n)\leq\alpha/8.
\]
No independence among the four events is needed.  A union bound proves
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}:
\mathcal C_P\neq\varnothing}P\{\text{all four bands hold}\}\geq1-\alpha.
\]

On these bands, fix \(u\in\mathcal C_P\).  Its restriction to \(\widehat B_n\) satisfies the level and pairwise Lipschitz inequalities.  At every support-mesh point \((d_j,z_j)\),
\[
|\widehat g_n(d_j,z_j)-u(d_j)|
\leq|\widehat g_n(d_j,z_j)-g(d_j,z_j)|+K|z_j|
\leq r_n+K|z_j|.
\]
The signed and moment bands give
\[
|J_P(u)-\textstyle\int u\,d\widehat\nu_n|\leq q_n,
\quad |T-\widehat T_n|\leq t_n,
\quad |A-\widehat A_n|\leq a_n.
\]
Also \(A\in[a_0,D_I]\).  Hence
\[
(u|_{\widehat B_n},J_P(u),T,A)\in\widehat{\mathscr F}_n
\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal C_P,
\]
so the last clause in the definition of \(\mathcal E_n(P)\) follows from the first four.  We have therefore proved the advertised uniform probability bound for \(\mathcal E_n(P)\).

The preceding inclusion immediately gives coverage by the raw ratio extrema.  Taking an optimizer of \(J_P\) at \(V_P^+\) and one at \(V_P^-\),
\[
\inf_{\widehat{\mathscr F}_n}\frac{t-j}{a}
\leq\frac{T-V_P^+}{A},
\qquad
\sup_{\widehat{\mathscr F}_n}\frac{t-j}{a}
\geq\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}.
\]
The true interval lies in \([-K,K]\), so endpoint clipping preserves these inequalities.  On \(\mathcal E_n(P)\) the feasible set is nonempty and the two raw extrema cannot cross; thus the reset rule is not invoked.

It remains to bound excess length.  Take any feasible \((v,j,t,a)\).  Extend the node vector to a bounded \(L\)-Lipschitz function \(E_nv\) on \(X_0\).  At a support point \(w=(d,z)\), choose a same-component mesh point \(w_j=(d_j,z_j)\) within \(s_n\).  The regression band, the relaxed mesh constraint, and the H\"older and Lipschitz inequalities give
\[
|g(d,z)-E_nv(d)|
\leq K|z|+\varepsilon_n,
\qquad
\varepsilon_n=2r_n+(K+L)s_n+Gs_n^\beta.
\]
Because \(s_n\leq h_n\) and \(r_n\geq Gh_n^\beta\),
\[
\varepsilon_n\leq3r_n+(K+L)s_n.
\]
Clipping stability supplies \(u^*=\Pi_P(E_nv)\in\mathcal C_P\) with \(\|E_nv-u^*\|_\infty\leq\varepsilon_n\).  Every observed \(X_i\) is a node, so \(E_nv(X_i)=v(X_i)\).  Using first the program's \(j\)-constraint, then empirical total variation one, and finally the signed band for the exact feasible \(u^*\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|j-J_P(u^*)|
&\leq\left|j-\int E_nv\,d\widehat\nu_n\right|
+\left|\int(E_nv-u^*)\,d\widehat\nu_n\right|
+\left|\int u^*\,d\widehat\nu_n-J_P(u^*)\right|\\
&\leq2q_n+\varepsilon_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Likewise \(|t-T|\leq2t_n\) and \(|a-A|\leq2a_n\).  Since both denominators are at least \(a_0\), and since \(|(T-J_P(u^*))/A|\leq K\),
\[
\left|\frac{t-j}{a}-\frac{T-J_P(u^*)}{A}\right|
\leq\frac{\varepsilon_n+2q_n+2t_n+2Ka_n}{a_0}.
\]
Every feasible ratio is therefore within this distance of some point of \(\Theta(P)\).  Applying the statement to minimizers and maximizers and combining it with outer inclusion proves that both endpoint gaps are nonnegative and bounded by this quantity.  Because \(A\leq D_I\), it is at most a fixed-class multiple of
\[
\frac{r_n+(K+L)s_n+q_n+t_n+Ka_n}{A}.
\]

For measurability, order the deterministic mesh nodes and the observed baseline coordinates lexicographically, removing duplicates by the first-index rule.  This is a Borel operation.  Cell counts, cell sums, and the empty-cell convention make every coefficient of the finite program Borel in \(\mathcal Z_n\).  Since \(a\geq a_0>0\), set \(c=1/a\) and multiply \((v,j,t,a)\) by \(c\); the constraint \(ca=1\) and all remaining inequalities are linear, which is the stated Charnes--Cooper transformation.  The transformed feasible set is a compact polytope.  For fixed \(n\), enumerate its finitely many possible active-constraint bases; on each Borel determinant stratum the associated vertex is a Borel rational function of the coefficients.  Taking the least objective value and then successively the least coordinate among ties selects the lexicographically least optimizer by finitely many Borel comparisons.  The maximum and reset rule are handled identically.  Thus \(\widehat L_n\), \(\widehat U_n\), and \(\widehat{\mathrm{CI}}_n\) are Borel measurable; no optimizer uniqueness is assumed.

Finally, \(N_n=O(h_n^{-2})\) and the declared bandwidth imply
\[
h_n^\beta
=O\!\left(\left\{\frac{\log n}{n}\right\}^{\beta/(2\beta+2)}\right),
\qquad
\sqrt{\frac{\log N_n}{nh_n^2}}
=O\!\left(\left\{\frac{\log n}{n}\right\}^{\beta/(2\beta+2)}\right).
\]
Also \(s_n\leq h_n\) and \(q_n,t_n,a_n=O(n^{-1/2})\).  Substitution in the endpoint bound proves the stated uniform rate.  Every construction used closed inequalities and deterministic boundary assignment, so density smoothness, strict feasibility, and optimizer uniqueness were nowhere required.

On \(\mathcal E_n(P)\), the uniform band-to-program theorem gives
\[
\widehat L_n\leq\frac{T-V_P^+}{A}
\leq\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}\leq\widehat U_n.
\]
The attained-interval theorem identifies the middle interval with \(\Theta(P)\), so
\[
\mathcal E_n(P)\subseteq
\{\Theta(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathrm{CI}}_n\}.
\]
Taking probabilities, then the infimum over compatible \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}\), and finally the lower limit gives
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}:
\mathcal C_P\neq\varnothing}
P\{\Theta(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathrm{CI}}_n\}
\geq1-\alpha.
\]
The deterministic inclusion \(\Theta(P)\subseteq[-K,K]\) shows that intersecting the empirical interval with \([-K,K]\) cannot remove a true value.  The parent theorem did not use \(R(P)>0\), strict inequalities, or unique optimizers, so the coverage statement includes singleton frontiers, binding obstacles, and nonunique solutions.

open_obligations.what_is_open: A matching minimax lower bound, uniform through \(R(P)\to0\), that separately attributes endpoint loss to learning the obstacle boundary and to learning the signed objective.
open_obligations.obstruction: The fixed regular-class assumptions give the upper-band ingredients but do not furnish a least-favorable family. The suggested shrinking-hole handle is not itself a proof of membership in the fixed known finite-rectangle support class, bounded Kullback--Leibler divergence, or optimized-endpoint separation.
open_obligations.attempted: The natural two-point route perturbs \(g\) by a local \(\beta\)-H\"older bump and changes the signed baseline mass. Keeping the known support and density bounds fixed while proving both legal-completion compatibility and a nonvanishing separation of the optimized endpoints requires an additional construction; assuming those properties would assume the crux.
open_obligations.partial_result: The proved upper bound is uniform and equals \(O(\{\log n/n\}^{\beta/(2\beta+2)}+n^{-1/2})\).  The frozen primitives do not provide a pair or hypercube of laws in the fixed known-support class whose Kullback--Leibler divergences and optimized-endpoint separations establish a matching lower bound, nor do they prove separate lower bounds for obstacle learning and signed-objective learning as \(R(P)\to0\).
